etymology: Originally a clinical term in PTSD therapy (a stimulus triggering a trauma response). Spread to broader culture in the 2010s, often used dismissively for anyone offended.
biblical_def: Modern: an involuntary distress response, sometimes a real PTSD trigger, often loosely a strong negative reaction. Biblical reframe: Scripture distinguishes between a wound that needs Christ's healing (real triggers) and a flesh that needs Christ's mortification (mere offense). Both are real categories; both have gospel answers.
webster_summary: An involuntary distress response, often loosely deployed.
webster_full: Originally a clinical term for a stimulus prompting a trauma-related distress response in PTSD. Mid-2010s onward extended in popular usage to describe any strong negative emotional reaction, often deployed dismissively ("snowflakes") or claimed self-justifyingly ("you triggered me"). The clinical and casual senses now coexist confusingly.
scriptures: Psalm 147:3
He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
Romans 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
Psalm 51:10
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
corruption_summary: Real trauma-triggers and ordinary offense get mashed into one category; clinical precision lost, gospel categories also.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic age has flattened a clinical category into a generic offense-claim. The result is twofold corruption: actual PTSD-triggers get dismissed as oversensitivity, and ordinary fleshly offense gets re-labeled as trauma to escape responsibility for the reaction.

Scripture distinguishes carefully. Real wounds need binding-up by the Healer (Ps 147:3). Fleshly reactivity needs mortifying by the Spirit (Rom 8:13). The gospel answers both, but it does not collapse them into one. Discerning which is which is part of pastoral and self-care wisdom.
roots_summary: From English trigger; clinical PTSD usage extended popularly.
usage: Distinguish wounds from flesh-reactivity.
Both have gospel answers; they are not the same answer.
Real trauma needs binding; flesh needs mortifying.

etymology: Cope: from Old French coper. Copium: 2010s internet coinage portmanteau of cope + opium — deployed to dismiss someone else's belief as wishful drug-like soothing.
biblical_def: Cope: to manage or endure. The slang copium dismissively names another person's reasoning as drug-like denial. Biblical reframe: Christians are commanded to endure (hypomenō) — not as denial but as faith rooted in resurrection. "Cope" alone is not a biblical category; endurance under hope is.
webster_summary: To manage, endure; slang "copium" mocks others' coping as denial.
webster_full: Cope: to contend, manage, endure. Internet slang "copium" (cope + opium) is deployed dismissively — you're just coping; you're sniffing copium — to label another's argument or hope as drug-like denial of reality. The dismissive form has overtaken the older neutral verb.
scriptures: Romans 5:3-5
Glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed.
Romans 8:24-25
For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it.
1 Peter 1:6-7
Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season... ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: That the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise.
corruption_summary: "Copium" weaponizes the dismissal of hope as drug-induced denial; Christian endurance gets re-categorized as pathology.
corruption_paragraphs: Internet culture frames hope itself as suspicious — if you trust the resurrection, you're sniffing copium. Scripture treats hope as the saint's lifeblood: "hope maketh not ashamed" (Rom 5:5). The cynic's mock is the world's cope.

Recover the biblical structure: tribulation produces patience, patience produces experience, experience produces hope. Christian endurance is not denial of present reality — it is faith in a future reality the cynic refuses to see.
usage: Endurance is hope's verb, not denial's.
The cynic mocks; the saint waits.
Hope maketh not ashamed.

etymology: Origin attributed to Ann Landers; popularized in 2010s social media as a dismissal: "X is living rent-free in your head."
biblical_def: Slang phrase used to dismiss someone's preoccupation with another person or idea as wasted mental real estate. Biblical reframe: Scripture diagnoses what occupies the heart as worship-direction. What "lives rent-free" in the mind is being granted authority. The remedy is not lighter mental load but reclaimed allegiance.
webster_summary: Slang for an unwelcome preoccupation occupying mental space.
webster_full: A modern phrase deployed dismissively to describe an unwelcome figure or idea that occupies someone's thoughts ("X is living rent-free in your head"). Implies the preoccupation is undeserved — the inhabitant has not earned the space they take up. Often used to mock political opponents.
scriptures: Philippians 4:8

Whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Proverbs 4:23
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
Colossians 3:2
Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
corruption_summary: The phrase is used to dismiss preoccupation as silly; Scripture treats mental tenancy as a serious moral category.
corruption_paragraphs: Pop culture mocks the preoccupied as foolish ("living rent-free"). Scripture treats the contents of the mind as a stewardship: what dwells in your thoughts shapes the issues of your life. The preoccupation isn't silly — it is revealing.
Recover the seriousness: take inventory of who lives in your head. Pay them no rent — evict them and move Christ in. Phil 4:8 is the eviction-and-furnishing list.
roots_summary: Modern English idiom; Phil 4:8 is the biblical reframe.
usage: Take inventory of mental tenants.
Evict; furnish with Phil 4:8.
Mental real estate is stewardship.

etymology: Literally "separated from hinges"; metaphorically, mentally unstable. In 2020s slang the term flipped polarity — "unhinged" became a compliment for chaotic, uninhibited self-expression.
biblical_def: Originally a description of mental instability; in current slang re-coded as positive aesthetic ("unhinged behavior," "unhinged tweet") — chaos as authenticity, restraint as fakeness. Biblical reframe: Scripture treats sōphrosynē (sound-mindedness, soberness) as virtue and ungoverned chaos as warning sign.
webster_summary: Mentally unstable; recently re-coded slangily as positive chaos-aesthetic.
webster_full: Disconnected from hinges; figuratively, mentally unstable; deranged. In 2020s slang the term flipped polarity: "unhinged" became a positive descriptor for content or behavior that abandons restraint — chaos as authenticity, lack of filter as virtue, derangement as compliment.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 1:7
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
Titus 2:6
Young men likewise exhort to be sober minded.
Proverbs 25:28
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
corruption_summary: Cultural inversion: instability re-branded as authenticity, restraint re-branded as repression. The polarity flip is the corruption.
corruption_paragraphs: When a culture re-codes "unhinged" as good, it has decided that instability is preferable to restraint — that chaos reads as truer than self-government. Scripture's teaching is the inverse: a man with no rule over his own spirit is a broken-down city. Walls are virtue, not repression.
Recover sōphrosynē: sound-mindedness, soberness, spirit-governed self. The Spirit's gift in 2 Timothy 1:7 is the opposite of unhinged. Re-hinge.
roots_summary: English compound; biblical opposite is Greek sōphrosynē.
usage: Sound mind is gift; unhinged is warning.
Walls are virtue; ruin is not.
Re-hinge under the Spirit.

etymology: Diminutive of "best friend," 2010s social media coinage. Often deployed performatively ("my besties!") to claim social proof rather than describe deep relationship.
biblical_def: Casual diminutive of best-friend, often performative. Biblical reframe: Scripture's category of friendship is heavier — covenant friendship (Jonathan and David), iron-sharpens-iron (Prov 27:17), "a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Prov 18:24). Most "besties" are not biblical friends; some biblical friends would never be called "besties."
webster_summary: Casual diminutive of best-friend; often performative.
webster_full: A modern affectionate diminutive of "best friend." Often used in plural for one's social circle ("my besties") or for any friendly bond, regardless of depth. The lightness of the word matches a cultural retreat from deeper friendship-language.
scriptures: Proverbs 18:24
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
Proverbs 27:17
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
John 15:13
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
corruption_summary: Lightens friendship-language to social-media stylings; the heavier categories of covenant friendship and iron-sharpening get displaced.
corruption_paragraphs: When friendship-vocabulary lightens, friendship itself often lightens with it. "Bestie" cannot bear the weight of Jonathan-and-David covenant or the iron-sharpens-iron friction of Proverbs 27. Some weights need a heavier word.

Recover the heavier vocabulary alongside the lighter: have besties if you must, but seek covenant friends — the brother-closer-than-brother kind — for the actual life-and-death work of soul formation.
roots_summary: English diminutive; biblical category is covenant friendship.
usage: Have besties; seek covenant friends.
Some friendships need iron-sharpening, not light banter.
Greater love — lay down life for friends.

etymology: 2010s dating-culture slang — a sudden physical revulsion at a romantic partner triggered by a small perceived flaw, after which attraction can't be recovered.
biblical_def: Slang for a sudden, disqualifying revulsion at a romantic partner over a trivial detail (their sneeze, their gait, their slang). Biblical reframe: covenant love is not at the mercy of momentary aesthetic recoil. Scripture's agapē is willed commitment that can outlast "the ick" by the thousand — because it was never first about being attracted.
webster_summary: Slang revulsion at a partner over trivial details, after which attraction can't recover.
webster_full: Modern dating-culture term for a sudden, often inexplicable physical revulsion at a romantic partner triggered by a perceived small flaw — their laugh, their gait, their pronunciation, their hobby. Typically framed as a one-way door: once "the ick" arrives, attraction is permanently lost. Implicitly treats romantic feeling as the foundation of relational viability.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 13:4-7
Charity suffereth long, and is kind... beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Ephesians 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.
Song of Solomon 8:7
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
corruption_summary: Builds romantic relationships on aesthetic-feeling rather than covenant commitment; "the ick" becomes the unappealable judge of viability.
corruption_paragraphs: When a culture treats sudden aesthetic revulsion as a relationship-ending verdict, it has decided that feeling is the foundation. Scripture builds covenant love on willed commitment instead — commitment that can outlast 1,000 "icks" because it was never anchored in feeling.

This does not mean ignoring red flags or staying in genuinely harmful relationships. It means recognizing that aesthetic revulsion at a quirk is a different category from discerning real incompatibility. The first is feeling; the second is judgment. Covenant love survives the first; wisdom heeds the second.
usage: Covenant love outlasts a thousand icks.
Distinguish revulsion at quirks from discernment of real incompatibility.
Feelings follow commitments, not lead them.

etymology: Borrowed from product-marketing ("soft launch" = limited initial release) into 2020s relationship-culture: a low-key, hint-only social media reveal of a romantic partner.
biblical_def: Modern social-media practice of revealing a romantic relationship through indirect cues (a hand in a photo, a back-of-head shot) rather than explicit announcement. Biblical reframe: covenant relationships are public commitments. Scripture's marriages have witnesses; vows are heard. The "soft launch" represents a culture afraid to commit publicly.
webster_summary: Indirect, hint-only social media reveal of a relationship.
webster_full: A 2020s social-media practice borrowed from product marketing: rather than explicitly announcing a new romantic partner, the relationship is hinted at through carefully ambiguous photos (a hand in frame, a partner's back, a captionless date). The hard launch (full reveal) may follow if the relationship survives. Functions as social-media-era ambiguity insurance against breakup-related embarrassment.
scriptures: Genesis 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Matthew 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Proverbs 31:23
Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land.
corruption_summary: Treats public commitment as risk to be managed rather than gift to be embraced; ambiguity preferred to vow.
corruption_paragraphs: Soft-launch culture is structurally afraid of public commitment. The hedging ambiguity protects against potential breakup-shame at the cost of never quite committing. Scripture's pattern is the opposite: vows are heard, witnesses gather, the husband is known in the gates.
Recover the vow's publicness. Yes-yes, no-no. Whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. A relationship hidden behind ambiguity is not yet covenant.
roots_summary: Modern marketing-borrowed term; biblical opposite is the publicly witnessed covenant.
usage: Vows are heard; covenants have witnesses.
Yes-yes, no-no; whatsoever is more cometh of evil.
Soft-launch is fear-of-shame culture.

etymology: Coined 2014 by Sophia Amoruso's memoir #Girlboss; surged through 2010s as feminist self-branding, declined late 2010s as the term became cringe / critique-bait.
biblical_def: Self-branded ambitious woman entrepreneur; the term peaked as feminist aspiration and crashed as critique-fodder when several prominent girlbosses' empires collapsed under harsh treatment of (often female) employees. Biblical reframe: Scripture knows ambitious capable women (Proverbs 31, Lydia, Priscilla) but binds their work to godly character — not self-branding.
webster_summary: Self-branded ambitious woman entrepreneur; rose and fell as feminist aspiration.
webster_full: A self-applied label for ambitious women in business or leadership, popularized by Sophia Amoruso's 2014 memoir. The term surged as positive feminist aspiration through the mid-2010s, then collapsed as multiple prominent girlbosses faced reckonings for treating employees harshly. By the early 2020s the term was largely cringe / critique-bait. "Girlboss, gatekeep, gaslight" became the late-stage parody.
scriptures: Proverbs 31:10-31
Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies... She considereth a field, and buyeth it... She maketh fine linen, and selleth it...

And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us... when she was baptized, and her household, she besought us, saying, If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide there.
Romans 16:3
Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Self-branded power-aspiration severed from character; "girlboss" framed ambition as identity rather than as character-tested capacity.
corruption_paragraphs: The girlboss-era promised that ambition + femininity = empire. The reality often included exploiting employees, performative wokeness, and cult-of-personality leadership. The Proverbs 31 woman is also industrious and entrepreneurial — but her capability is bound to fear-of-the-LORD, character, and care for those under her.

Recover the binding: ambition without character produces collapse. Scripture's industrious women (Proverbs 31, Lydia, Priscilla) work hard, run businesses, lead households — but the work is bound to godly character, not self-branding.
roots_summary: Modern coinage; biblical answer is the Proverbs 31 woman.
usage: Capability + character — not capability as identity.
Read Proverbs 31 instead of Girlboss.
Lydia ran a business; she also opened her home.

etymology: From financial cancellation language extended to social ostracism through 2010s social media; "cancel culture" denotes the practice of mass-revoking the social license of a person whose past statements or actions are deemed unacceptable.
biblical_def: To revoke someone's social standing en masse for past statements, actions, or beliefs deemed unacceptable. Biblical reframe: Scripture distinguishes between just church discipline (Matt 18:15-17, with restoration as goal), and crowd-driven excommunication (Pilate's crowd, the Sanhedrin's verdict on Christ). Canceling lacks both Matthew 18's process and its restorative aim.
webster_summary: To revoke someone's social standing through mass online ostracism.
webster_full: The 2010s-2020s practice of mass-revoking a person's social license — their platform, employment, public welcome — as collective punishment for statements, actions, or beliefs deemed unacceptable. Cancel culture distinguishes itself from criminal justice in lacking due process, from church discipline in lacking restoration as goal, and from accountability in often outlasting genuine repentance.
scriptures: Matthew 18:15-17

Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone... but if he will not hear, take with thee one or two more... and if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church.
Galatians 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness.
John 8:7
He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.
corruption_summary: Crowd-driven excommunication without process or restoration; lacks both Matthew 18's structure and its restorative aim.
corruption_paragraphs: Cancel culture mimics church discipline without its essentials. Matthew 18 has a process (private, then witnessed, then public); cancel culture skips to public. Galatians 6:1 has a goal (restoration in meekness); cancel culture has no goal beyond punishment. The result is mob justice with religious-sounding rhetoric.

This is not to dismiss accountability. Scripture demands it. But the form matters: Matthew 18's process protects against false accusation, gives space for repentance, and aims at restoration. Cancel culture protects nothing and aims at nothing — except the satisfaction of the crowd.
roots_summary: Modern usage; biblical answer is Matthew 18 and Galatians 6:1.
usage: Discipline aims at restoration; cancellation aims at punishment.
Matthew 18 has process; cancel culture skips to crowd.
Without due process, accountability becomes mob.

etymology: From the Greek myth of Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection; clinical psychology took up the term for self-absorbed personality patterns; popular usage now applies it widely.
biblical_def: Excessive self-focus and self-love. Clinically: a personality disorder marked by grandiosity, lack of empathy, and need for admiration. Popularly: deployed widely as diagnosis-by-internet for difficult relationships. Biblical: the heart curved-in-on-itself (Augustine's incurvatus in se) — the universal fallen condition that grace alone uncurves.
webster_summary: Excessive self-focus; clinical disorder; popular over-diagnosis.
webster_full: From Greek myth (Narcissus enchanted with his reflection); adopted by clinical psychology for personality patterns marked by grandiosity, lack of empathy, hypersensitivity to criticism, and need for admiration. Clinical Narcissistic Personality Disorder is rare and serious. Popular usage has expanded the term to cover any difficult or self-absorbed person, often diagnosing absent ex-partners and family members through internet checklists.
scriptures: Philippians 2:3-4

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
2 Timothy 3:1-2
This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers.
Luke 9:23
If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.
corruption_summary: Real clinical narcissism gets confused with universal fallen self-love; over-diagnosis weaponizes the term against difficult people.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors: (1) Real Narcissistic Personality Disorder gets dismissed as "everyone's like that." (2) Ordinary fallen self-love gets weaponized as "narcissist" against family members, exes, or political opponents. Both lose the precision the term once had.

Scripture's diagnosis is broader and more honest: every fallen heart is curved-in-on-itself (incurvatus in se). Some people have particularly virulent expressions of this (NPD). All people are subject to its gravitational pull. The cure is not better self-diagnosis but daily self-denial under the cross.
roots_summary: Greek myth; biblical answer is Philippians 2 lowliness.
usage: Distinguish clinical NPD from universal self-love.
Don't diagnose by internet checklist.
Daily self-denial uncurves the heart.
